# Global Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing Programme
## Recommendation for the Steering Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. No section is deferred; where a number cannot honestly be fixed before the diagnostic reports, it is shown as a gate parameter with the date and the person who will set it (§12.6, §16).**

**Circulation:** steering group, for decision. Prior circulation to the seven category leads, the four plant directors, Group Legal, Group Trade Compliance, Group Reporting and the Chief Financial Officer's office. **Not yet for supplier communication. Expressly not yet for any external, customer-facing or investor-facing statement** (§10.1).

---

### How we would ask you to use this

Three notes, then the substance.

**First, what changed from v1.0 and why.** The reviewers were right on three points that went to the design rather than to the drafting, and we would rather record that plainly than absorb it quietly.

1. v1.0 offered a single waiver route across all five floors. That was wrong. A standard concerning forced labour cannot carry a waiver, and an internal register recording that an officer of this company approved a twelve-month departure from one would be a document read back to us in a customs proceeding or an NGO report. The floors are now split into **two classes** — non-derogable and progressive — and only the progressive class has a flexibility route, which is now a dated closure plan rather than a waiver (§3, §3.8).
2. The disclosure amnesty in v1.0 promised more than we are lawfully able to promise. It now covers **commercial consequence only**, with scheduled legal exclusions, material substitution removed to its own route, a concealment carve-out, and a records architecture to be agreed with Legal and the external auditor before a single supplier hears the word (§3.7).
3. The failure test was built on AND-logic and could almost never have fired. It is now OR-logic on the substantive proxies, with coverage-based rather than absolute-dollar metrics, and with thresholds set after the diagnostic produces a baseline rather than invented before it (§8.6).

**Second, the cards.** The cluster cards in §6 are **working hypotheses about supply structures and site conditions, offered so that they can be corrected**. They describe patterns we have observed in supply flows, not countries and not the people who live in them. Where a category lead or plant holds real diagnostic data — an unannounced assessment, a worker-voice sample, a qualification study — that data supersedes the card and the card is retired for that flow (§5.4). A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

**Third, two courtesies we would ask the steering group to extend before this travels further.**

- That the seven category leads, the four plant directors and the two engineering chiefs see §§3, 4, 9 and 13 and have time to respond in their own way, through their own line, before the board pack is assembled. A programme that devolves sourcing judgement and then arrives in a category fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else.
- That §10 be walked through with Group Legal, Trade Compliance, Group Reporting and the external auditor **before any part of this is described to a supplier**, and that no wording from this paper migrate into a sustainability statement, customer questionnaire response or investor deck without the sign-off route in §10.1. The single likeliest cause of avoidable damage here is not a supply failure. It is a well-meant public commitment that becomes a disclosure liability, or a supplier questionnaire that creates a written record we cannot later stand behind.

*A note on suppliers themselves: v1.0 designed a supplier-facing architecture without consulting a supplier, while arguing that programmes arriving fully formed contradict themselves. That inconsistency is corrected in §11.5 — a supplier advisory panel of nine, convened before Gate 2, with two seats reserved for Tier-2 firms.*

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: five sourcing floors, split into non-derogable and progressive classes; supplier selection, remediation sequencing, buffer design and local partnership devolved to categories and plants beneath a mandatory-uniform contract layer and single-point supplier ownership; a bounded disclosure amnesty that treats supplier-found problems as intelligence; an engineering design-for-resilience workstream, because single-sourcing is created at specification and not in procurement; four instrumented pilots; and a published protocol binding our own buying conduct to the same discipline we ask of suppliers. Approve the diagnostic and mobilisation now; approve the full envelope at a named gate when the baseline exists.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Scale anchor** (absent from v1.0) | Revenue $4.1B; COGS $2.94B; direct materials and components spend **$1.42B**; 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers across 38 countries; 4 plants; 7 categories. Indicative full-programme spend of $17.6M Y1 is **1.24% of direct spend** and **0.43% of revenue** **[O]** |
| Global mandate — **Class A, non-derogable** | Freely-given labour and worker-pays-nothing (Floor II core indicators); prohibition of retaliation against a worker who raises a concern (Floor III core). **No waiver, no register entry, no alternative form.** Escalation and remediation only (§3.3, §3.4) |
| Global mandate — **Class B, progressive** | Traceability depth of critical flows; grievance-channel maturity; qualified-alternative capability; responsible-exit sequencing. Each has a **dated closure plan** route, approved and reviewed, never an open-ended waiver (§3.8) |
| Devolved to categories & plants | Supplier choice within the approved-vendor frame, remediation sequencing, buffer sizing, local partners, capability-building design, and the language in which any of it is described to suppliers — beneath a **mandatory-uniform contract layer** and **single-point supplier ownership** (§4.5) |
| The engineering half | **Design-for-resilience workstream** co-owned by Engineering: second-source-ready specification standard, part standardisation, qualification-cycle compression, dual-tooling policy at part-approval gate (§7.5). This was the largest omission in v1.0 |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots** — one deep-tier opaque flow; one single-source long-qualification part; one high-agency-labour site cluster; one recently-acquired plant's inherited supply base — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | **Our own procurement and forecasting incentives**, not supplier resistance (§8.1). Cost-down targets, forecast bias and change-order volatility will defeat this faster than any supplier will **[J]** |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published buyer-conduct protocol**, quarterly: our forecast bias by category, payment-term behaviour, audit visits imposed per supplier, change-order frequency, and every reversal of a devolved sourcing decision with written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision (§9) |
| Element we would defend | **12-month bounded disclosure amnesty** (§3.7): commercial consequence waived for self-disclosed Tier-2s, recruitment-fee findings and labour findings; legal consequence never waived; scheduled exclusions; substitution excluded and routed to Quality (§3.7.3) **[J]** |
| Measurement | 70% operational and worker-verified proxies, 30% declared and audit scores **[J]**; audit-score inflation correction with a **stated method** — unannounced-audit delta, worker-voice divergence coefficient, auditor-firm fixed effects, shrinkage on small n (§8.4) |
| Numeric failure test | **OR-logic**, five substantive conditions; a rising audited-compliance index is an **aggravating** condition, not a gate. Thresholds set at Gate 2 from the diagnostic baseline. Firing the test pauses the programme and stops further capital (§8.6) |
| Money — one view, not two | **Total cost of ownership, Years 1–3: $58.7M**, comprising programme opex $29.7M; buffer and qualification-inventory carrying and obsolescence cost $9.4M; one-off working-capital build $46M (balance sheet, ~$19.6M residual after Y3 unwind). Funding routes and governance differ and are shown separately **on the same page** (§12.2) |
| Of which supplier capability funding **we** pay | **$5.8M** across two years — the line most often cut first, and the one whose absence has ended comparable programmes elsewhere **[J]** |
| Funding split | Central funds diagnostic, traceability platform, upstream mapping, worker-voice channels, remedy fund, pilot facilitation. Plants and categories fund qualification and dual-tooling with a **65% central offset in Y1, 35% in Y2, nil thereafter** **[J]** (§12.4) |
| Decision architecture | **Two gates, not one.** Gate 1 on **22 April**: approve $2.41M for diagnostic, mobilisation, engineering scoping, worker-voice pilot and legal records architecture. Gate 2 on **15 July**: full envelope, pilot scope, critical-input list, failure thresholds (§12.6) |
| Decisions requested now | **Three** — §12.7 |
| Governance | CPO sponsor; COO co-accountable; **CFO joins the steering group** (working capital); **Chief Sustainability & Reporting Officer joins** (CSRD/disclosure); named tiebreak to the CEO on the two decisions we expect to stall (§10.7, §12.8). Programme director reports to the CPO with a dotted line to the COO, sits in Group Strategy, holds delegated authority to $500K (§12.8) |
| Immediate actions requiring no approval | Four, owners named, all closed within 30 days (§1.3) — including the **54 Tier-1 suppliers who never signed the code and continued to supply** |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Resilience is a purchased option rather than an attitude; and responsible sourcing is an information problem before it is a compliance problem. **[J]** — considered practitioner assertion, not a finding. The steering group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement; the key is at §14 and is now applied throughout rather than decoratively.

The failure we are trying to avoid is documented in our own last three years: a supplier code signed by 1,780 of 1,834 Tier-1 suppliers **[O]**; an audit pass rate above 90% **[O]**; and two disruptions in eighteen months that neither the code nor the audits anticipated, both originating below Tier 1 **[O]**, with combined recovery cost of $23.6M and 41 days of line stoppage across two plants **[O]**. That combination is not a coverage gap. It is evidence that we have measured the wrong things accurately.

### 1.2 What we are not claiming

We are not claiming that this programme prevents disruption. It shortens recovery and reduces the number of surprises **[J]**. We are not claiming it makes the supply base ethical; it makes conditions in it visible and gives us a route to act, which is a smaller and more honest claim **[J]**. And we are not claiming the floors are enforceable at every tier — §4.2 sets out, tier by tier, where we hold leverage and where a floor is honestly **observational** rather than enforceable. v1.0 blurred that line, and blurring it would have embarrassed us in front of the very colleagues we need.

### 1.3 Four things we would close before the steering group next meets

These need no funding and no decision. We list them because the steering group would reasonably ask why they were not already done, and because it would be poor form to hold them inside an eight-figure proposal.

| # | Action | Owner | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The 54 unsigned Tier-1 suppliers.** Establish, supplier by supplier, whether each still supplies, what it supplies, whether any sit on the critical list, why signature was never obtained, and whether a purchase order was placed without terms. Report by name to the steering group | Head of Supplier Governance | 21 days |
| 2 | Confirm which of our own customer contracts contain flow-down clauses that would be breached, or notification obligations triggered, by anything in §3.7 (amnesty) before any supplier hears of it | Group Legal | 30 days |
| 3 | Baseline our own payment-term behaviour against contracted terms by category, and our forecast bias over eight quarters. This is the raw material for §9 and we should know it before we ask anyone else anything | Group Treasury with Category Planning | 30 days |
| 4 | Confirm whether any part on the current critical list is sourced from a site subject to UFLPA entity-list exposure or an equivalent designation | Trade Compliance | 14 days |

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would ask the steering group to test

The initiative is described as *supply chain resilience and ethics*. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **visibility and decision-latency** problem in a resilience costume, compounded by an incentive problem of our own making. Only some of the candidate drivers below respond to supplier requirements, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What a code, audit programme and clause cascade do to it | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| We do not know who is in Tier 2–4 for critical flows | Nothing — requires paid mapping and a reason to disclose (§3.7) | **[O]** both 2023–24 disruptions |
| We know, but the information does not reach the person who could act | **Amplifies harm** — confident sourcing decisions on stale data | **[A]** to be tested |
| Single-source parts with multi-year qualification cycles | Nothing — needs capital, tooling and engineering time, not policy | **[O]** 61 parts, mean qualification 9.4 months |
| Single-sourcing designed in at specification stage | Nothing — belongs to Engineering, not Procurement (§7.5) | **[J]** |
| Suppliers have capability gaps rather than intent gaps | Improves *only if* paired with funded capability support (§8.5) | **[A]** |
| Our cost-down targets pay suppliers to conceal problems | Noth
